pr_body:
This test runs CRDB both against the regular clock and ptp clock,
verifies that CRDB won't start against an invalid (non-existent) PTP
clock, and also verifies that if the system clock is changed while
running against a proper PTP clock, the system continues to function
normally.

It would've been preferable to change the PTP clock as opposed to the
system clock, but this seems difficult to achieve.

Fixes: https://github.com/cockroachdb/cockroach/issues/108273

Epic: none
Release note: None

Epic: none
Fixes: https://github.com/cockroachdb/cockroach/issues/108273

```go
func monotonicUnixNano() int64 {
	monoTime.Lock()
	defer monoTime.Unlock()

	now := timeutil.Now().UnixNano()
	if now <= monoTime.last {
		now = monoTime.last + 1
	}
	monoTime.last = now

```

```go

```

Code is more than ten years old! Time to freshen it up and plumb a clock down there to see if that helps.

I'm running now with an extra commit that teaches gossip to use the `ptp` clock. The first 30 runs passed; going for another 30 now and I'm assuming ~they're going to pass as well~ (edit:) _wrongly that the gossip fix is enough - it's not._

There are more than 700 other non-test callers to `timeutil.Now()`. Each of these will pull from the system clock instead of the PTP one. The system time is used all over the place. So even if this test passes, we are still a far cry from consistently using the `ptp` clock.

What I don't entirely understand is: wouldn't a deployment that uses the ptp clock also synchronize the system clock with that ptp clock? So they should be ~equal, and this would be less of a "big deal" than it initially sounds.

Of course this test winds the system clock back an hour relative to the ptp clock, so it might hit all sorts of weird snags over the years.

issue_context.title: util/timeutil/ptp: add end-to-end test
issue_context.body:
We should add an end-to-end test for the PTP clock using an actual PTP device (or at the very least, a mocked device file). This would possibly be a roachtest.

Jira issue: CRDB-30405
comments:
Just as a note as I was looking at this, to reproduce a "vMotion move" - you can run something like:

`kill -STOP $PID ; sleep .5; kill -CONT $PID`

Modifying the sleep time to simulate how long you want to freeze the process. 

I did verify that if `server.clock.forward_jump_check_enabled` is enabled and this is run it will cause a process crash even though the clock stays perfectly synced on a node. 
This is somewhat expected, because any place where we read the current clock and then process it after we pause will cause the problem. 

We should be careful about claiming that a PTP clock with vMotion will not result in stale reads (this was one of their questions to us) - as when a node is stalled, it can return a result that is inconsistent with the physical clock. 

I did not see the process panic when the setting was disabled.
In https://github.com/cockroachdb/cockroach/pull/108552#discussion_r1298672652, @darinpp suggests enabling a KVM PTP device, which should provide sufficient coverage for an end-to-end test.

I'm going to pick this up.

I was able to get the following to work:

```
# Spin up roachprod instance.
$ ./bin/roachprod create travers-test -n 1 -c gce
$ ./bin/roachprod stage travers-test release v23.1.11
$ ./bin/roachprod ssh travers-test:1

# Install package including ptp_kvm.
$ sudo apt-get install -y linux-modules-extra-$(uname -r)

# Activate kernel module.
$ sudo modprobe ptp_kvm

# Confirm existence of PTP device.
$ ls -l /dev/ptp*
crw-r--r-- 1 root root 246, 0 Oct  6  2023 /dev/ptp0
lrwxrwxrwx 1 root root      4 Oct  6  2023 /dev/ptp_kvm -> ptp0

# Alter perms - cockroach needs to be able to read from the device.
$ sudo chmod 0644 /dev/ptp0

# Alter the system time to something far enough in the past.
$ sudo date --set '20200101 00:00'
$ date -u
Wed Jan  1 00:00:01 UTC 2020

# Boot cockroach, using the PTP device.
$ ./cockroach start-single-node --store $(mktemp -d) --insecure --logtostderr --clock-device /dev/ptp0

# In a second shell, fetch the time.
$ ./cockroach sql --insecure
#
# Welcome to the CockroachDB SQL shell.
# All statements must be terminated by a semicolon.
# To exit, type: \q.
#
# Server version: CockroachDB CCL v23.1.11 (x86_64-pc-linux-gnu, built 2023/09/27 01:53:43, go1.19.10) (same version as client)
# Cluster ID: ea4d78dc-ebe0-4883-b2c2-1cdb74a470cd
#
# Enter \? for a brief introduction.
#
root@localhost:26257/defaultdb> select now();
               now
---------------------------------
  2023-10-06 21:46:09.445993+00
(1 row)

Time: 1ms total (execution 0ms / network 0ms)
```

Confirm that the time is obtained from the PTP device.

---

Next step, turn this into a roachtest.

Yeah, we'd also want to run a workload on the cluster for a little while to ensure nothing bad happens.

I wonder if we can make this metamorphic across all/most roachtests, by injecting a PTP clock device and messing up the system clock. That way, we can check that other functionality doesn't have implicit dependencies on the system/external clocks, stuff like backups/changefeeds/etc. We can split that out as a separate issue though, don't have to block this on it.

I worked on this a bit today. I have a basic roachtest (#129123) that sets up  the ptp0 device (following Nick's recipe above), starts without it, stops, starts but pointing at an invalid file for a ptp device and verifies startup fails, then starts again this time pointing at the correct device.
I still have to see what can be added to verify that we're actually using the ptp device. Messing with the system clock as "proof" of that is something I expect to be brittle. I'd much rather install a "pipe" device that we can intercept, or use bpf, or whatever. But if we're trying to be comprehensive I'm not sure we can do much better than messing with the system clock.
We may find a need to be pragmatic about how deeply we test this.

> I'm not sure we can do much better than messing with the system clock

This might require some diving into PTP devices and Linux clock, but it looks like we could do something like mount a "slave" device and point it at the "master" PTP clock device (`/dev/ptp0`). The [`phc2sys`](https://linux.die.net/man/8/phc2sys) tool could then be used to re-synchronize the "slave" with an arbitrary offset (`-O` flag).

I could imagine a test doing something like:
- Mount a slave into each node, each with offset 0 from the master.
- Boot CRDB.
- Assert everything functioning a-ok.
- Pick a node and re-synchronize it's slave clock with some nasty offset.
- Assert that node panics due to clock drift.

One could also conceivably set all nodes' slave PTP clocks well into the future / past with a well known offset (i.e. set all a year into the future). That gives you a means of asserting that the PTP clock is being used (i.e. check that `select now()` is within some bounds of `time.Now() + KNOWN_OFFSET`). This would also flush out any dependencies on the system clock.

review_comments: Do you want to have this run nightly for a while to get some miles on it? Then we can drop to weekly? No strong opinion.
I'll run it in CI for 30 times instead, if there's noise I'd rather catch it before merge.
